Peter I. Known as Peter the Great, he transformed Russia from a semi-feudal Eurasian power into a modern European empire. His methods were brutal, his vision unwavering, and the result was a state remade in the Western image.

He began with a Grand Embassy between 1697 and 1698, traveling incognito to Western Europe to study shipbuilding, engineering, and military science. He returned convinced that Russia must westernize or perish. He mandated westernization edicts: nobles were required to shave their beards and adopt Western dress, a radical break with Orthodox tradition that scandalized the conservative clergy. He reformed the church itself, subordinating the patriarch to a secular governing board called the Holy Synod, making the Russian church an instrument of state power.

Militarily, he modernized the Russian army along Western lines, replacing feudal levies with a standing conscripted force. He then fought the Great Northern War between 1700 and 1721 against Sweden's Charles XII. He struggled at first but eventually defeated Sweden and established Russia as the dominant Baltic power. The turning point came at the Battle of Poltava in 1709. Sweden's decline cleared the way for Russian hegemony in Eastern Europe.

To secure his newly won Baltic position, he founded St. Petersburg in 1703 as a window to the West, building it on captured Swedish territory. He created a modern Russian navy, transitioning the state from an inland river power to a seagoing strength. He moved the capital from Moscow to St. Petersburg, symbolizing the turn toward Europe.

Domestically, he centralized power ruthlessly. In 1722, he established the Table of Ranks, a hierarchy tying nobility status to state service rather than birth, breaking with feudal precedent. He conducted military campaigns in the Caucasus and Caspian region, expanding the empire southward. His succession was fraught with violence. He had his own son Alexei executed in 1718 on suspicion of plotting against him.

Peter the Great embodies the enlightened absolutist archetype: he willed Russia into modernity through state coercion, accepting the suffering of his people as the price of imperial greatness. His methods were brutal and his success was undeniable. The template he created—top-down modernization, state terror in service of progress, naked will-to-power—became the blueprint for later Russian leaders, from Catherine the Great to Stalin. He is the hinge on which Russia turns from East to West.
